request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

PAIR 1:
A: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response object, and the code then reads `res?.data` — a property that does not exist on a fetch Response — so token is undefined. `token.access_token` throws TypeError (Cannot read properties of undefined) inside refreshAccessToken, turning a refresh under credential-sharing mode into an unhandled 500 on the booking path instead of a token refresh.
B: With credential sharing enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response, but this code reads res?.data (the googleauth response shape), so token is undefined and token.access_token throws a TypeError — and the sync response body is never read, so the shared token is never applied. On any deployment with CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set, every Google Calendar token refresh crashes; the operation falls back to the expired token and Google Calendar availability/booking calls fail with auth errors until the app is reinstalled.

PAIR 2:
A: The minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`, which evaluate to literal property names "z.string()"/"z.string().optional()" rather than validating arbitrary token fields, so the schema only enforces access_token and validates nothing else. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED, any provider response — including malformed ones missing refresh_token, expiry, or with wrong types — passes validation, and garbage credentials get persisted to the DB.
B: When credential sharing is enabled, full per-app schema validation (zoomRefreshedTokenSchema, refreshTokenResponseSchema, googleCredentialSchema, salesforceTokenSchema) is discarded in favor of the broken minimum schema, so garbage or malformed token payloads are accepted whenever they contain an access_token. A credential-sync endpoint returning malformed data (missing instance_url for Salesforce, expiry_date for Google, etc.) passes validation, corrupt credentials get persisted via prisma.credential.update, and subsequent API calls fail in provider-specific ways instead of being rejected at refresh time — validation weakened on the sync path with no requirement justifying it.
